items.title: We haven’t seen the last of the major tech outages
items.summary: Over the last week or so, we have seen a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage that brought entire companies to a standstill, and a banking outage at JPMorgan Chase. But the consensus is that there are more to come. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton t
items.content:
Microsoft and the US government agree there are more outages to come.

Over the last week or so, we have seen a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage that brought entire companies to a standstill, and a banking outage at JPMorgan Chase . But the consensus is that there are more to come . Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN :

“The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.”

Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning about further outages to CBS , but sounded a much more ominous tone.

“I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn’t the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks … The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now.”

While the outages over the last week were believed to be caused by cyberattacks, Smith said that AI has made it easier to find flaws , “and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems,” he said.

The last few months have also seen an increase in attacks on government and commercial systems, including those at the USDA , JP Morgan , and supermarkets .

Whether outages are brought on by AI-assisted hackers or human error during the rush to patch an aging system , one thing seems certain: there will be more in the coming months.

items.content:
오픈AI가 AI의 지능 발전 수준을 측정할 수 있는 사전학습 성능 수치를 공개하고, 이를 토대로 주요 AI 기업들이 공동으로 지켜야 할 개발 제한선을 마련하자고 제안했다. 학습 성능이 높아질수록 예상하지 못한 새로운 능력이 나타난다는 분석으로, 샘 알트먼 CEO도 최근 회사가 발표한 내용 중 가장 중요한 것이라고 평가했다.

야쿠브 파초키 오픈AI 최고과학책임자는 22일(현지시간) ' 퍼플렉시티와 지능(Perplexity and Intelligence) '이라는 글을 발표하고, AI의 지능 발전을 추적할 수 있는 공통 지표와 개발 제한선을 마련해야 한다고 주장했다.

파초키는 AI의 지능을 형성하는 핵심 과정이 방대한 데이터에서 다음 단어나 토큰을 예측하도록 훈련하는 사전학습에 있다고 설명했다. 이후 진행하는 미세조정이나 강화학습 등은 이 과정에서 형성된 잠재 능력을 특정 작업에 활용하도록 끌어내는 역할을 한다는 것이다.

이를 뒷받침하기 위해 내부에서 측정해 온 모델별 학습 성능 수치를 공개했다. 핵심 지표인 '퍼플렉시티(Perplexity)'는 AI가 처음 접하는 문장에서 다음에 나올 단어나 토큰을 얼마나 잘 예측하는지 평가하는 지표다. 오픈AI는 이를 로그값으로 변환한 '로그 퍼플렉시티'를 사용했으며, 수치가 낮을수록 예측 성능이 뛰어나다는 의미다.

오픈AI의 내부 코드 데이터셋을 기준으로 'GPT-3.5'는 약 0.99를 기록했으며, 'GPT-4'에서는 약 0.91까지 낮아졌다. 이후 이 수치가 0.8 아래로 내려가면서 사이버 보안과 수학 등에서 기존 모델과 질적으로 다른 능력이 나타났다고 설명했다.

특히 약 0.76에 도달한 모델은 오랫동안 해결되지 않았던 수학 문제에서 획기적인 연구 성과를 내기 시작했다. 파초키는 "오랫동안 고민해 온 수학 문제들이 하나의 슬랙 대화창에서 연달아 해결되는 모습을 보는 것은 매우 비현실적인 경험이었다"라고 말했다.

그는 이러한 추세가 이어지면 로그 퍼플렉시티가 0.68~0.70 수준에 도달할 때 또 다른 획기적인 능력이 등장할 수 있다고 전망했다. 어떤 능력이 나타날지는 현재 알 수 없으며, 기존 벤치마크로는 이를 미리 포착하지 못할 가능성도 있다고 설명했다.

공개한 그래프에는 'GPT-6.2 아스트라'보다 로그 퍼플렉시티가 더 낮은 약 0.73의 미공개 내부 모델도 등장했다. 이는 오픈AI가 공개 모델보다 성능이 높은 모델을 내부에서 평가하고 있다는 의미다.

이처럼 올해 학습 성능은 이전보다 빠르게 향상됐지만, 이는 주로 장기간에 걸친 인간 연구자들의 노력과 컴퓨팅 투자에 따른 것이라는 설명이다. AI 자동화의 기여는 아직 상대적으로 작지만, 최근에는 AI가 모델 설계에 의미 있는 기여를 한 사례도 나타나기 시작했다.

파초키는 앞으로 AI가 사전학습 알고리즘 자체를 개선하는 역할까지 맡게 되면 발전 속도가 한층 빨라질 수 있다고 전망했다. 인간 연구자를 완전히 대체하지 않더라도 AI가 연구에 참여하는 것만으로 큰 변화가 가능하며, 최근 수학 연구에서 나타난 급격한 성능 향상이 AI 연구에서도 재현된다면 이르면 2027년부터 관련 기술의 근본적인 혁신이 연달아 등장할 수 있다는 것이다.

문제는 AI의 발전 속도에 맞춰 안전 기술도 같은 속도로 발전한다는 보장이 없다는 점이다. 파초키는 AI가 안전성 연구와 감시 기술 개발에도 기여하겠지만, 학습 기술의 발전 속도를 따라잡기에는 충분하지 않을 수 있다고 판단했다.

이에 따라 그는 퍼플렉시티와 다른 성능 지표를 토대로 AI 개발의 공동 제한선을 설정하자고 제안했다. 기업들이 합의한 지능 수준을 넘어서는 개발을 자제하고, AI의 행동을 이해하고 감시할 수 있는 기술이 구체적인 목표에 도달하면 다음 단계로 넘어가는 방식이다.

오픈AI가 경쟁상 민감한 내부 학습 성능 수치를 공개한 것도 이런 공동 기준을 마련하기 위해서다. 파초키는 경쟁사에 자사의 기술 수준을 알려주는 부담이 있지만, 업계가 안전 기준을 마련하는 일이 더 중요하다고 설명했다.

알트먼 CEO는 X를 통해 이번 제안을 공개적으로 지지했다. 그는 "오픈AI가 최근 발표한 것 중 가장 중요한 내용"이라고 평가하며, 업계가 공동 제한선에 합의하는 것이 AI의 "안전과 통제"를 확보하는 데 도움이 될 것이라고 밝혔다.

Pretraining should just be called “training”. You can’t have pre and post, but never have actual training. Like, you dress up to work out and then you shower, but don’t actually work out

Unless I’m super missing something, data starvation will be the training challenge next…

일론 머스크 CEO도 파초키의 게시물에 답글을 달아 "사전학습은 그냥 '학습'이라고 불러야 한다"라며 "내가 뭔가 크게 놓치고 있는 게 아니라면 내년에는 데이터 부족이 학습의 주요 장애물이 될 것"이라고 전망했다. 대규모 데이터 학습이 AI 발전의 핵심이라는 인식은 파초키와 통하지만, 머스크는 안전성보다 학습 데이터 부족을 향후 기술 발전의 주요 제약 요인으로 지목했다.

파초키는 지난 9월에도 AI가 스스로 성능을 개선하는 '재귀적 자기개선(RSI)' 단계에 진입할 가능성을 경고하고 자발적인 개발 속도 조절을 촉구한 바 있다. 이번에는 당시의 문제의식을 학습 성능이라는 기술 지표와 구체적인 개발 제한 방안으로 발전시킨 것이다.

퍼플렉시티가 AI의 모든 능력을 측정할 수 있는 것은 아니다. 기업마다 학습 데이터와 평가 방법이 달라 수치를 직접 비교하기 어렵고, 강화학습이나 추론 기술을 통한 성능 향상은 이 지표에 반영되지 않는다는 한계가 있다. 최초 제한선을 어느 수준에서 설정할지, 언제부터 시행할지도 정해지지 않았다.

이번 제안은 AI 모델의 학습과 추론, AI를 활용한 연구 등 다양한 분야에서 기술 발전이 빨라지는 가운데, AI의 지능 발전을 측정할 공통 기준을 마련하고 업계 차원의 안전장치를 구축해야 한다는 요구를 다시 제기했다는 의미가 있다.

items.title: OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development
items.summary: To establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how to measure speed.
items.content:
A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity.

Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”

But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name ) could be that measurement.

In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.”

Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5.

“GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.”

So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.”

From value creation to value extraction

By Tim O’Reilly November 20, 2026 • 32 minute read

On October 16, 2026, I delivered the second Annual Margaret Levi Lecture in Political Economy in conjunction with the AI and History conference at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. This is my original lecture as written, which incorporates material from many pieces I’ve written over the years. As delivered, I departed significantly from the script, as you can see from the embedded video below or the transcript that you can see at the link above.

It’s an honor to give a lecture in Margaret Levi’s name. I’ve been asked to reflect on the changes in the political economy of Silicon Valley throughout my 40-plus year career in and about it, and I can’t imagine a better framing for my remarks than Margaret’s vision.

Margaret understood that advances in our ability to work together are essential to a better future. Cooperation is the human superpower. She also asks what happens when the systems of cooperation we have constructed over time stop holding up their end of the bargain.

That is very much the question that Silicon Valley is facing today. An industry that pioneered advances in collective intelligence at scale used to engender love from its customers because of the way it solved new problems in their lives. It now too often inspires fear and loathing. How did things go so wrong?

But let me start with my own history. I started my company more than 40 years ago with a $500 initial investment. We took in no venture capital, and we built a business that now generates hundreds of millions of dollars in profitable annual revenue, funded by customers who love our products and pay us for them. We got there the slow way, through steady organic growth. That is quite anathema to the rush to the top of whatever appears to be the latest hill that seems to characterize Silicon Valley today. Even when climbing that hill traps a company at a local maximum, the hope is to get to payday before the industry moves on to the next hill.

My original corporate goal was stated as simply “Interesting work for interesting people.” That evolved into two principles: “Change the world by spreading the knowledge of innovators,” and “Create more value than you capture.” Those principles shaped not only my company but what I expected the internet to be. When we launched GNN , the Global Network Navigator, in 1993, it was the first web portal and the first ad-supported site on the World Wide Web, and for two years it was the place people went to find other sites. What we built was a machine for pointing you at the best of what other people had made, and then getting out of your way.

Even our idea of advertising was not what you think of today. It was inspired by direct mail advertising, where you’d read articles in a print magazine or look at accompanying ads, and then you’d call an 800 number or circle a number on a “bingo card” that you’d send in to the publisher so that the advertiser could send you a brochure. I realized that the web would be a good replacement for that awkward system, that every company ought to have its own website that provided more information about its products and services. What we invented was not the “grab your attention” kind of advertising. It was all about utility, and sharing information that customers really wanted and needed. In short, it was the commercial web, which no one any longer thinks of as advertising, even though it is the most durable and useful kind.

The commercial web was only a small part of what the web became. The web was the playground of amateurs, not entrepreneurs. It was a marvelous collective work of human imagination, creativity, sharing, and ultimately (though that became toxic only later), competition for attention. Our hand-curated catalog of the best websites was soon surpassed by algorithmic solutions like those provided by Google. The amount of content produced was far larger than purely human curation could manage. It was an early example of what Richard Sutton was later to call “the bitter lesson” in his analysis of AI training.

In my 2005 essay “ What Is Web 2.0? ” I described how the companies that survived the dotcom bust had all, in one way or another, figured out how to help people navigate the resulting information explosion at scale. As Herbert Simon noted in 1971, an abundance of information leads to a scarcity of attention. In the face of increasing information abundance, he predicted that we would use machines to help us better allocate our time and attention. And so it has transpired: Information has become so abundant that it defies manual curation. Instead, powerful, proprietary algorithmic systems use the data they collect to match users with the answers, news, entertainment, products, applications, and services they seek. Today’s AI is in many ways a continuation of this arc.

I called this “harnessing collective intelligence.” All of it was, in economic terms, a set of remarkable advances in networked, data-enabled market coordination. It felt like a public good even when it was privately owned.

items.title: The Birds of GTA 6: A Field Guide to Vice City and Leonida's Wildlife
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.audubon.org/magazine/birds-of-gta-6-field-guide-vice-city-wildlife Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50602843 Points: 297 # Comments: 122
items.content:
I finished collecting the bricks of cocaine and landed my bullet-ridden seaplane at the dock. It was time for birdwatching.

A few minutes after midnight on Thursday morning, I joined millions of other gamers for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI , the latest in the smash video game series from Rockstar Games. The new installment is already a worldwide sensation, earning more than $1.8 billion in revenue the day it was released.

Grand Theft Auto , or GTA , games are famous for their “open worlds,” which allow players to explore massive, intricately detailed versions of America. Much of that exploration is focused on mayhem and chaos: The story missions usher players through criminal underworlds, and players are at any time free to steal cars, rob stores and pedestrians, and initiate anarchy.

But GTA 6 has more going on than just criminality—it’s also a world filled with wildlife. Previous GTA games were set in fictionalized versions of New York City and Hollywood, but the new one returns to Vice City, its version of Miami, which was also the setting for 2002’s installment. Unlike that game, however, GTA 6 ’s South Florida is complete with dozens of species of birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, mammals, and other creatures. The in-game Progress menu tracks all kinds of items to find, including 338 vehicles, 205 weapons, and, of primary interest to me, at least 60 bird species.

I made it my mission to find them all as quickly as possible.

(Side note: Pre-release marketing for GTA 6 touted 62 bird species, but the official birds Progress screen only lists 60, with a handful of others listed on the hunting screen.)

I am one hour in and I’ve found 16/60 birds https://t.co/81x42O1BuY

— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026

You begin the game as Jason, a low-level criminal working to raise money to support his young family. You’re equipped with zoom binoculars before the very first mission—tracking drug runners through a swamp and escaping with the seaplane—and I used them immediately, stopping mid-lurk to scan some Double-crested Cormorants on a dock. (Distracted from the job at hand to look at birds—just like real life!) They looked like Double-crested Cormorants!

After the first mission the player is free to explore the entirety of the map, stealing cars, robbing stores, or just birding wherever they want. The game makes birding easy: Looking at any bird through the in-game binoculars gives players the option to hold a button to “study” it, thereby adding it to the Progress menu. Simply standing on the back deck of Jason’s first safehouse yields a bunch of species like Brown Pelican and Laughing Gull. It’s just like being in South Florida!

Looking south from the back deck, I spotted another bird perched on an adjacent dock, with a few people gathered at the end. Looking through my binoculars I spotted my first Herring Gull —and noticed that the people, a woman and three men, were fully and visibly naked. Jason apparently lives next to a nudist resort. It’s just like being in South Florida!

Two down, 58 to go. I found a few more species right in Jason’s backyard, including American Crow, House Sparrow, and South Florida-appropriate Monk Parakeets, before venturing out into the huge map. My strategy for finding birds in GTA 6 was the same as finding birds in real life: look in as many habitats as I could find. I started by “borrowing” a fanboat off a nearby dock and heading back to the swampy areas near the seaplane mission. There were tons of birds across the open water and in the marsh: Caspian Terns, Mottled Ducks, Sanderlings, Spotted Sandpipers, Great Blue Herons, Glossy and White Ibis, and … flocks of Whooping Cranes?

incredibly healthy populations of critically-endangered Whooping Cranes across Vice City. Huge if true. https://t.co/doe6oMOvBX

In fact, I found a number of avian inaccuracies in just my first few hours of playtime. Certain species like Whooping Crane and Red-cockaded Woodpecker are common throughout the map, despite being endangered and threatened, respectively, in real life. Golden Eagles are extremely rare in Florida, but I found one soaring over the Mt. Kalaga area (mountains, one may point out, aren’t found in Florida either). Some species have confusing naming quirks—the chickadee is Black-capped instead of Carolina, and there’s a “New World Oriole” instead of a Baltimore Oriole—but those changes are likely due to the fact that Carolina and Baltimore don’t exist in the GTA universe.

Though some of the inaccuracies may feel like a letdown in a game that is being hailed as the Greatest of All Time , I think it’s important to remember that it’s also game where you can get a ride from a dog driving a jet ski . Grand Theft Auto games are meant to be fun, not science. Plus, despite some of the misfires, the avifauna feels well thought-out. The map is true to the ecological boundaries of South Florida, with herons, gulls, and other waterbirds in the south while birds like Red-bellied Woodpecker, Wood Stork, and American Robin are found farther north. Birders know that certain exotic species have made their home in tropical South Florida, including Spot-breasted Oriole and Red Junglefowl, both in the game.

That geographic fidelity is the main tip for anyone looking to check off all the game’s birds: Find their habitat. The game doesn’t tell you what species to look for, so you’ll need to cover a lot of ground to find everything. Wading birds, shorebirds, and seabirds are common in the southern coastal part of the map. A number of smaller, open-country or forest birds are found up north. Owls come out at night. Birds in zoos and domestic farmyard birds count towards the 60, too, so don’t overlook those areas.

Wild Boar roadkill. It’s just like birding in Florida! https://t.co/gT84IticOK

items.title: Delta flights in and out of Atlanta delayed due to system outage
items.summary: All Delta flights in and out of Atlanta are facing significant delays on Sunday due to a problem with the system that calculates a plane's weight and balance. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is Delta's largest hub and one of the busiest airports in the world. Whi
items.content:
Major delays for Delta come just a week after a nationwide groundstop.

All Delta flights in and out of Atlanta are facing significant delays on Sunday due to a problem with the system that calculates a plane’s weight and balance. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is Delta’s largest hub and one of the busiest airports in the world. While only Delta is impacted at the moment, disruptions at Hartsfield-Jackson could potentially affect other airports and airlines if delays continue to pile up.

The issues with Delta’s systems in Atlanta come just one week after an FAA outage led to a nationwide groundstop and thousands of canceled flights. According to The New York Times :

The system that went offline calculates the total weight of an airplane, including its airframe, fuel, passengers and their baggage. The system also allows pilots to determine the plane’s center of gravity and whether the weight is evenly distributed — data points that help ensure safe passage.

“Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said in a statement on Sunday.

items.title: Binding of Isaac developer removes AI music from Repentance Plus
items.summary: The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music. Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. They found se
items.content:
Creator Edmund McMillen claims he ‘had no idea’ AI music was used in the latest version of Binding of Isaac.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music . Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto -themed section. They found several audio files with Suno metadata that pointed back to the tracks on Suno’s site.

Creator Edmund McMillen took to X to apologize and claimed he “had no idea” the in-game GTA parody used generative AI music. Adding to the drama, Valve requires developers to disclose how and when they use generative AI in the development process, and Nicalis, Inc., the studio behind Repentance Plus , doesn’t appear to have mentioned the AI music anywhere.

Within hours of the discovery, Nicalis shared on X that Repentance Plus had been updated and the generated music files had been removed . While reviews on Steam have yet to rebound, and the game is still rated as “overwhelmingly negative,” users on X seem to be giving McMillen the benefit of the doubt, likely because he’s been quite outspoken on AI in game development, calling it “ uninspired and bland ” in a TikTok from 2024.

items.title: Perplexity and Intelligence
items.summary: Article URL: https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50601525 Points: 446 # Comments: 302
items.content:
By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI

From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently ⁠ (opens in a new window) , predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared ⁠ (opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “ an alien mind ⁠ ”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset. 2 , 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets 4 , GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.

As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.

A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.

We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements 5 . While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.

items.title: TechCrunch Mobility: A/B testing robots vs. humans
items.summary: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and, now more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
items.content:
Waymo pulling its robotaxis off freeways (again) and Zoox robotaxis launching on the Uber app illustrate the push and pull between progress and setbacks in the autonomous vehicle industry.

There are signs of growth. For instance, Tesla has now surpassed Waymo in Texas in the number of robotaxis registered with the state (Tesla has 1,507 and Waymo has 1,345). But does that translate to market dominance?

A better metric, if we’re trying to gauge who is leading, would be commercial driverless miles. And if we’re measuring cost-efficiency, another useful metric would be driverless miles per vehicle. By those measures, Waymo is still ahead, based on data available to me. But with Waymo’s recent freeways setback and Tesla’s push to expand its robotaxi fleet with Cybercabs, that lead could shrink.

Not that there needs to be a winner, by the way. Transportation is deeply fragmented, and there is room for multiple players in the U.S., not to mention the rest of the world.

A recent discussion with my Autonocast co-host Ed Niedermeyer, whose book, “Elon Take the Wheel,” comes out December 1, got me thinking about how Las Vegas could soon become a real world A/B test of sorts for human-driven vs. autonomous ride-hailing services.

Uber, as mentioned above, just added Zoox to its ride-hailing app in Las Vegas. For now, riders don’t have much of a choice. Uber customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi, and they can always decline a robot ride. But they can’t directly select a robotaxi. Instead, Uber riders will be matched with one if it’s available.

Uber said that will soon change. The company plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November.

Las Vegas will also become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app, he said. (Hyundai’s self-driving subsidiary Motional is also an Uber partner.)

That would give Uber riders a meaningful choice: a human driver or a robotaxi, and potentially even which autonomous service to use. And it could offer a revealing look at what customers actually prefer when given that choice. Price could tip the balance, too.

It makes me wonder whether Las Vegas will become the next battleground for organized labor as robotaxis begin competing directly with human drivers.

You might have seen the Wall Street Journal scoop that General Motors is working with an executive search firm to identify possible candidates to replace CEO Mary Barra . Rumors of her imminent departure have swirled for months, but this time there appears to be real work happening behind the scenes.

I reached out to a few little birds to learn more and here’s what they’re telling me. And, for the record, GM declined to comment.

GM has hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles, according to one source, who noted it’s possible that the board has other executive search firms working on this as well. The board is taking a two-track approach to its search, which is occurring simultaneously.

The first is focused on traditional yet transformative automotive CEOs. One name that has come up from the executive search firm is José Muñoz, who is president and CEO of Hyundai. The board is also interested in someone less traditional. The firm has apparently floated names like Doug Field, who recently became CEO of Mind Robotics, and Larry Culp of GE, according to a source with direct information.

There are internal GM folks who are also in the mix, including Sterling Anderson, co-founder of self-driving trucks company Aurora who became chief product officer at GM in May 2025, and Paul Jacobson, the company’s executive vice president and chief financial officer.

Got a tip for us? Email Kirsten Korosec at [email protected] .

Elysian Aircraft , the Dutch aerospace company developing aviation electrification technologies, raised €12 million in private and public funding from FideFlux, SecFund, and ROM InWest, as well as from individual investors and family offices.

Mahindra Last Mile Mobility , an electric three-wheeler business under Mahindra & Mahindra, is looking at an IPO in about 18 months, per Bloomberg .

Numa , a startup developing an AI operating system for dealerships, raised a $45 million Series C round led by New York-based Blue Cloud Ventures. Threshold Ventures, Costanoa, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures, and Tokio Marine Future Fund also participated.

Stark Future , a European electric motorcycle company, raised at least €150 million in equity, Reuters reported. The raise was led by Highland Europe, alongside Morgan Stanley Investment Management’s 1GT and Axon Partners Group.

Vincue , an automotive tech company that sells software to dealerships, raised $93 million in a round led by Wavecrest Growth Partners, with continued backing from FM Capital.

Also , the electric micromobility startup that spun out of Rivian last year, has paused deliveries of its new e-bike over problems with its software and batteries, The Verge reported .

Edmunds released new data that found the average new vehicle is selling for a record $50,087.

Redwood Materials is using computer vision and machine learning to identify and sort batteries by chemistry before they’re fed into the company’s rotary calciner — a massive cylindrical industrial furnace used to process 40,000 metric tons of raw feedstock a year.

Tesla said it will spend about $3.3 billion to expand its Berlin gigafactory to produce Cybercabs — yet another signal of the company’s global autonomy ambitions.

items.title: Open Social Web Alliance
items.summary: Article URL: https://osw-alliance.net/en/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50600511 Points: 206 # Comments: 206
items.content:
How do we build social media that strengthens democratic discourse and is both resilient and appealing?

The Open Social Web Alliance aims to provide the answers.

A shared, standardised communication protocol: it may sound technically complicated, but it is as simple as it is brilliant, and the technical blueprint has long been familiar to all of us: email. Whether your address is hosted by Proton, Posteo, Gmail or GMX, your digital letters reach their destination. This is the idea we build on.

The year is 2028. Thanks to smart investment and political foresight, the Open Social Web has achieved its breakthrough. More than 100 million people connect, communicate and experience the world of open social networks. No platform economy à la Meta, ByteDance, Alphabet and co., no stressful digital moves and no toxic design. It works just like email: whether on Mastodon, Eurosky’s Mu or Streamplace, you have one account, your own posts and content, your own choices, and the freedom to connect with 100 million users worldwide.

A critical mass of users in Europe has turned its back on the platform monopolies and created a free market built on interoperable infrastructure. Today, users decide for themselves which content, which algorithms and which applications they want to use. Closed platforms have become open networks. On the ActivityPub and AT Protocol protocols (as well as Matrix for direct messaging), an ecosystem of non-commercial, public service and commercial offerings has emerged. They enrich and complement public-interest projects such as Mastodon and Eurosky, and they communicate with one another through shared interfaces.

This vision describes the Open Social Web (OSW): a decentralised, public-interest infrastructure for digital communication, based on open standards and interoperable protocols.

The idea of an Open Social Web is not new. The Fediverse has been in development since 2008 and is home to diverse, vibrant communities that build individual applications and run instances. While its focus has so far been on Europe, North America and Japan, there are now more than 100 applications, such as Mastodon, Loops and PeerTube, and more than 42,000 active instances worldwide. Even so, the number of active users, around 13 million, is growing only slowly. The ATmosphere community has been developing since 2022, primarily in North America but increasingly in Europe and beyond. It currently has around 43 million registered accounts and dozens of implementations and applications, such as Eurosky’s Mu, Gander and Sill.

For many reasons, both protocol-based social networks are attractive alternatives to the platform economy dominated by Meta, ByteDance and Alphabet. So why have people been so hesitant to switch?

We have identified five key challenges: infrastructure, governance, funding, appeal and public mandate. Below, we set out how we can overcome them and make the Open Social Web Alliance a shared success.

An ecosystem like this does not emerge on its own. Our roadmap shows how the Open Social Web could reach a relevant scale within just a few months. It takes political will, smart regulation, sufficient funding and a broad coalition of actors willing to share responsibility. The task is big. But the levers are there.

As a first step, we are founding the Open Social Web Alliance: an open alliance of stakeholders from civil society, research, business, media, culture and the public sector who are committed to the shared governance of the OSW. It brings together a wide range of existing communities and initiatives and is to be supported in future by a publicly funded secretariat. Its central goal: building and operating the OSW’s core infrastructure (see Section 2.1, Infrastructure).

Our roadmap envisions that the German federal government will explicitly support the Alliance, for instance by acting as patron of an Open Social Web Summit in autumn 2026, to which everyone with an interest in the OSW would be invited.

At the summit, the Alliance would adopt its charter, setting out how it admits new members and how it intends to implement its governance going forward (see Section 2.2, Governance). By spring 2027, public funding for the infrastructure would be in place, along with a first core funding round of public and private capital for innovation and applications (see Section 2.3, Funding). The Alliance would publish its first Social Web Health Report, featuring findings from user surveys, legal, technical and academic analyses, and clear recommendations for further development (see Section 2.4, Appeal). In parallel, the federal and state governments would ensure that the legal basis for cooperation between public service media, other media, business and civil society is established (see Section 2.5, Public Mandate). The federal government would also champion the OSW idea at EU level, for instance through an implementation push for effective digital legislation. As key stakeholders such as the federal government adopt OSW applications as their primary channel of communication, influential creators and publishers would follow suit, and central political debates would quickly shift to the Open Social Web. Taken together, these measures would reduce the influence and appeal of today’s dominant Big Tech platforms.

The Open Social Web Alliance is looking for allies: people and organisations who are convinced that genuine social networks can create real value.

We look forward to hearing from you. Got better ideas than ours? Even better!

items.title: Protesters storm Meta offices in India
items.summary: Members of the opposition Congress party protested outside Meta's offices in Delhi on Friday and appear to have entered the building in a video shared by CNN. Members of the party's youth wing are demanding the company restore accounts of party leaders and warned of more protests
items.content:
Members of the youth wing of the Congress party are demanding its leaders’ Instagram accounts be reinstated.

Members of the opposition Congress party protested outside Meta’s offices in Delhi on Friday and appear to have entered the building in a video shared by CNN . Members of the party’s youth wing are demanding the company restore accounts of party leaders and warned of more protests to come. The Congress party has criticized Meta for censoring speech that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his BJP party disagree with, and has placed banners accusing Mark Zuckerberg of favoring BJP around the city.

While two accounts in question were restored Friday, Manu Jain, who oversees social media for the party’s youth wing, told Reuters that “thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted.”

In February, India issued tighter rules around the removal of “unlawful” content, changing the timeline from 36 hours to just three. Modi and the Indian government have long been criticized for their restrictive policies around free speech and accused of stifling opposition viewpoints and attempting to bully the press.

Meta did not immediately return a request for comment.
